html:
Ceylon is the old European name for Sri Lanka, the island off the southern tip of India. On the map it covers the island from 1650 to 1938, the centuries when European powers held its coasts and then all of it.

Three powers came in turn:

  • The Portuguese arrived in 1505 and held forts and cinnamon lands along the coast (Portuguese Ceylon).
  • The Dutch East India Company drove them out between 1638 and 1658, first as allies of the hill kingdom of Kandy. They then ran the coast themselves as Dutch Ceylon.
  • Britain took the Dutch coast in 1796 and Kandy in 1815, so the whole island came under one foreign ruler for the first time. This was British Ceylon.

The British turned the hills into plantations. Coffee boomed from the 1830s until coffee rust wiped it out after 1869, and tea took its place. Planters brought in Tamil workers from south India (Tamil workers to Ceylon estates), whose descendants still live in the hill country. A Buddhist revival, led by figures such as Anagarika Dharmapala, fed a growing national feeling.

In 1931 Ceylon got universal suffrage, one of the first colonies in Asia to do so. It became independent in 1948 and took the name Sri Lanka in 1972.
